title: Shraddha Kapoor Disappears Into a Tamasha Legend. The Eetha Teaser Is the Boldest She Has Ever Been.
excerpt: Hard-locked into Cocktail 2 prints this Friday, the first look at Laxman Utekar's Vithabai biopic refuses the massy hero entry — and that restraint is exactly why it lands.
body:
The crowd is screaming for her. They want the entrance — the slow-motion turn, the swirl of skirt, the chest-thumping massy reveal that Bollywood has trained us to expect every time a leading lady is summoned by name. **Eetha**, they chant. And then **Shraddha Kapoor** walks on, and it is nothing like that at all.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=uzcn_PbrLmM</youtube>

That refusal is the whole point. The teaser for *Eetha* — attached to the prints of *Cocktail 2*, which poured into cinemas this Friday — runs two minutes and eighteen seconds, and it spends every one of them telling you that the Shraddha you think you know is not the one you are about to meet. She plays **Vithabai Narayangaonkar**, the legendary Marathi Tamasha artist whose voice and footwork defined a folk art form, and from the first frame she vanishes into the woman. The dance is not decoration here. The expressions are not a showreel. This is an actress doing the unglamorous, terrifying work of becoming someone real.

> "Shraddha Kapoor has essayed a powerful, author-backed role and will be seen in a never-before-seen avatar." — industry insider, to Bollywood Hungama

Let's be honest about the stakes. Shraddha has spent a decade as one of Hindi cinema's most likeable stars — the *Aashiqui 2* heartbreak, the *Stree* franchise's box-office muscle, the girl-next-door warmth that sells tickets without ever demanding the critics take her seriously. *Eetha* is the swing. A period biopic, set in the dust and lantern-light of the Maharashtrian Tamasha circuit, built entirely on her shoulders. If it works, it rewrites what she's allowed to play for the rest of her career.

The man betting on her is **Laxman Utekar**, and he is on the hottest streak in the industry. His *Chhaava* was the phenomenon of 2025, and he follows it here with a subject that could not be more different — no Maratha war drums, just a woman, a craft, and a country that adored her before it forgot her. The supporting bench is serious: **Randeep Hooda**, who knows a thing or two about physical transformation, and the reliably excellent **Mohammed Zeeshan Ayyub**. Maddock Films is steering it to an August 28 release, landing it squarely on Raksha Bandhan.

The CBFC passed the teaser with a U/A 13+ on June 17, and you can feel why Maddock chose *Cocktail 2* as the launchpad. The studio has turned the attached-teaser into an art form — *Bhool Chuk Maaf* rode out with *Chhaava*, the *Stree 2* prints carried *Chhaava*'s own first look. A packed Friday house for a Shahid–Kriti–Rashmika romcom is the widest possible net, and it drops a regional-flavoured biopic in front of an all-India crowd that might otherwise never have found it. Alongside *Eetha*, audiences also caught the first tease of **Rajkummar Rao**'s *Prahaar – The Ujjwal Nikam Story*, due August 7. Maddock is loading its August like a slingshot.

What makes *Eetha* feel different from the usual transformation-bait is the discipline of the teaser itself. There is a Maharashtrian earthiness to the colour palette — ochres, deep reds, the warm grain of a stage lit by oil and ambition. The folk music throbs underneath. And Shraddha, instead of arriving as a star, arrives as a performer mid-life, mid-craft, carrying the weight of a real woman's story. The grapevine calls her work here raw and completely unlike anything she's done. The teaser doesn't argue with that.

For the diaspora, this is one to watch the dates on. Maddock's recent titles have had strong overseas theatrical rollouts across the US, UK and Canada, and an August 28 Raksha Bandhan release is prime festival-weekend counter-programming for NRI audiences who plan their cinema trips around the calendar back home. Expect advance bookings in New York, London and Toronto to open close to release, with a streaming window — likely Netflix or JioHotstar, in keeping with Maddock's pattern — to follow weeks later for those who can't make the theatre.

The smart money said Shraddha couldn't carry a film this heavy alone. The *Eetha* teaser is her first answer, and it is a quietly thrilling one. Come August, we find out if she can sustain it for two hours. On this evidence, I wouldn't bet against her.
